strengths: The task is practically motivated: combining a reference image with a description of changed attributes can support person retrieval when either modality is insufficient. ITCPR provides a potentially useful benchmark with 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three existing datasets.

The two-stage framework is coherent and relatively simple. Person-specific encoder fine-tuning followed by lightweight textual inversion enables composed retrieval without training on composed-query triplets. The distinction between triplet-free training and supervised person image–text training is reasonably clear.

The improvements over simple fusion are substantial. With ViT-L/14, Table I reports 45.913% Rank-1 and 55.630% mAP, compared with 32.016% and 41.831% for image–text averaging using the same fine-tuned encoders. This supports the usefulness of learned composition within the evaluated setting.

The experiments cover two backbone sizes, alternative supervision, training-data quantities, mapper architectures, prompts, token counts, and ensembles. Optimization settings and runtime measurements provide useful implementation information.
weaknesses: The central comparison with existing textual-inversion methods is inadequately controlled. Table I and Section V-B indicate that Pic2Word and SEARLE retain mapping networks trained with the original CLIP parameters when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. Word4Per instead trains its mapper specifically for those encoders and person data. This mismatch confounds algorithmic improvements with domain adaptation and representation compatibility. Retraining the closest baselines under matched encoders and training data is necessary to substantiate the headline superiority claim; this is the main reason for rejection.

Methodological originality is limited relative to the cited work. Image-to-pseudo-word mapping and composition through a frozen text encoder closely follow Pic2Word/SEARLE, while encoder fine-tuning uses established similarity-distribution and identity losses. The distinctive additions are person-domain adaptation and identity/text supervision. These could be useful, particularly alongside the benchmark, but their contribution beyond a properly adapted existing method remains unresolved.

The evaluation does not establish a clean model-selection protocol. ITCPR is explicitly designated for testing, yet its results are used to select mapper depth, width, and prompt configuration. No separate validation split or independent final evaluation is described. The absence of repeated runs or uncertainty estimates also makes the smaller differences between supervision choices, prompts, and ensembles difficult to assess.

Benchmark reliability needs stronger documentation. False-negative correction uses a visual encoder to retrieve top-k candidates for manual inspection, but the encoder, k, annotator agreement, and verification criteria are unspecified. Reviewing retrieved candidates does not establish that all relevant gallery images were found. Because the benchmark is a principal contribution and incomplete positives directly affect retrieval metrics, the annotation procedure and its residual error require validation.

The mechanistic explanations exceed the evidence. Figure 9 visualizes the frozen visual encoder upstream of TINet, so it cannot establish that text-supervised inversion suppresses background information. Figure 10 provides only a few illustrative retrieval examples. Controlled background perturbations or quantitative attribute-preservation tests would better support the claimed distinction between visual and textual supervision.

The proposed release of a real-person retrieval dataset and the stated public-security applications require an explicit account of source-image reuse and redistribution permissions, privacy protections, and potential misidentification or surveillance harms. The manuscript does not provide this documentation or discussion. This is an ethical reporting gap, rather than evidence of a demonstrated violation.
